A yew is a type of tree — or sometimes a large shrub — that grows in many parts of the world, especially across Europe, Asia, and North America. It belongs to a group of very ancient plants that have existed on Earth for millions of years.

A yew is an evergreen plant, which means it keeps its leaves throughout the year and does not shed them in winter. Its leaves are small, flat, and needle-like — dark green on top and paler underneath. They are arranged neatly in two rows along the branches, giving the tree a feathery, layered appearance.

The yew produces small, berry-like fruits that are bright red and waxy, shaped like little cups with a seed sitting inside. These are not true berries in the botanical sense — they are called arils — but they look like red jewels dotting the dark green branches, making the tree quite striking in appearance.

The bark of a yew tree is reddish-brown and tends to be thin, scaly, and peeling.

Yews are generally medium-sized trees, often growing to about 10–20 metres tall, though some can grow much larger. They grow very slowly — far more slowly than most other trees. This slow growth, however, is part of what makes them remarkable.
Why is the yew famous for its age?

The yew is one of the longest-living organisms on Earth. Some yew trees in Britain and Europe are believed to be 3,000 to 5,000 years old, making them among the oldest living things on the planet. This extraordinary lifespan, combined with the fact that the tree stays green even in the dead of winter, has made the yew a powerful symbol of eternity, immortality, and death across many cultures for thousands of years.

Because of this symbolism, yew trees are traditionally planted in churchyards and cemeteries in Britain and parts of Europe — a tradition so old that many ancient yews actually predate the churches they stand beside. When you see a very old churchyard in England, there is a good chance a massive, ancient yew tree is growing in it.

Yes — and this is critically important. The yew is one of the most poisonous trees in temperate climates. Almost every part of the plant is toxic: the bark, the leaves (needles), and especially the seeds inside the red fruits. The toxic substances inside yew are called taxine alkaloids, and they attack the heart, potentially causing cardiac arrest and death in both humans and animals.

Horses, cattle, deer, and other grazing animals can die if they eat yew foliage. Even a relatively small amount of yew needles can be fatal.

The one exception is the bright red, fleshy part of the aril (the cup-like covering around the seed). That fleshy part alone is not toxic and is sweet-tasting. However, the seed inside it is highly toxic, so eating the fruit whole or chewing the seed is dangerous. For this reason, you should never eat anything from a yew tree unless you are absolutely certain of what you're doing.

The word "yew" is also used to refer to the wood of the yew tree. Yew wood is dense, hard, and uniquely elastic — meaning it can flex and spring back without breaking. Because of this quality, yew wood was historically the preferred material for making longbows, particularly the famous English longbow used in medieval warfare. The longbow made from yew was one of the most powerful and accurate weapons of its time, and it played a decisive role in famous battles like Agincourt in 1415.

Today, yew wood is also used in fine woodworking, furniture, and decorative objects, where its rich reddish-brown colour and fine grain are prized.

Here is something surprising: the yew tree, despite being poisonous, has given the world one of its most important cancer-fighting drugs. Scientists discovered that a chemical found in the bark and needles of a North American species (the Pacific yew) could kill cancer cells. This substance was developed into a drug called paclitaxel (sold under the brand name Taxol), which is now widely used in the treatment of breast cancer, lung cancer, and ovarian cancer, among others. So while the yew can kill a living thing through its natural toxins, it has also been adapted to save human lives.

Yews are found naturally across a wide range:

  • Europe (especially Britain, Ireland, and the Mediterranean region)
  • North Africa
  • Asia (including the Himalayas, China, and Japan)
  • North America (especially the Pacific coast)

They prefer cool, temperate climates and often grow in forests, on hillsides, and on rocky ground. They are shade-tolerant, meaning they can thrive even under a canopy of larger trees. Yews are also very commonly planted in gardens because they respond well to trimming and shaping — topiary artists have long used yews to create elaborate sculpted hedges and animal shapes.

A yew is a slow-growing, extremely long-lived evergreen tree with dark needle-like leaves, distinctive red berry-like fruits, and highly poisonous bark, needles, and seeds. Its wood is elastic and historically famous for making longbows. It is culturally associated with death and immortality, commonly found in old European churchyards, and has contributed to modern medicine through the cancer drug paclitaxel. The word "yew" can refer both to the living tree itself and to the wood taken from it.
